title: Hurricane season peaks today. What's fact and what's fiction.
text:
Hurricane season peaks today. What's fact and what's fiction.
- September marks the historical peak of the Atlantic hurricane season, not the end of it.
- Hurricane impacts like high winds and flooding can extend hundreds of miles inland, affecting more than just coastal areas.
- Even newer homes can have vulnerabilities, so all homeowners in hurricane-prone regions should take preparedness seriously.
Contrary to popular belief, September marks the historical peak of Atlantic hurricane season. This means hurricane season is not only upon us, but in its prime time. If you live in a hurricane zone, home prep and maintenance are likely top of mind.
To find out what matters most to homeowners in the path of a hurricane, USA TODAY talked to Dr. Ian Giammanco, the managing director of atmospheric science and lead research meteorologist for Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS).
With so many people living in hurricane central, one of Dr. Giammanco's biggest concerns is the continued growth in hurricane-prone areas. "As more homes are built in these regions, the potential for insured losses continues to increase," he says. "At the same time, many residents are new to hurricane risk and may be preparing for their first storm."
Here, USA TODAY explains how to prepare your home for a hurricane, busting one myth about hurricanes at a time.
Myth No. 1: Hurricane season is almost over by September
Atlantic hurricane season may begin as early as June 1st, but the worst of the season is generally August through the end of October, with the peak happening around September 10th. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, this time period accounts for 78% of the tropical storm days, 87% of the category 1 and 2 hurricane days and as much as 96% of the major (category 3, 4 and 5) hurricane days.
The reason? Warm ocean temperatures and atmospheric conditions (such as high humidity and unstable air temperatures that change rapidly) make the perfect storm for hurricane development.
"Many people think of hurricane season as something that starts in June and is winding down by late summer. In reality, the seasonal peak is around September 10," says Dr. Giammanco. "Historically, some of the most impactful storms occur in August, September, and October, which is the peak of the Atlantic season when ocean temperatures are at their warmest and atmospheric conditions are often favorable for hurricane development."
Myth No. 2: Wind is the biggest danger during every hurricane
While the 100+ mile-per-hour winds may seen like the largest threat during a storm, it's actually the water that you need to worry about.
Storm surges, flooding from heavy rain, tornadoes and rip currents pose the most significant risks to your life and home.
"Storm surge is what drives many evacuation orders, so it's important for homeowners to know whether they live in a surge zone and understand their local evacuation plans before a storm threatens," Dr. Giammanco says.
Myth No. 3: Only coastal homeowners need to worry
Think living in a land locked zone saves you from hurricane damage? Think again.
"Hurricane impacts extend well beyond the shoreline," Dr. Giammanco says. "High winds, tornadoes from tropical systems, and wind-driven rain can cause significant damage hundreds of miles inland."
Even homes that sit far away from the water can still experience high winds, flooding, heavy rain and fires. It's not unheard of for a hurricane to travel 100 to 200 miles inland, and hurricanes have been known to span coast to coast in Florida, for example.
Moral of the story: "Every homeowner in a hurricane-prone region should take preparedness seriously, regardless of how close they live to the coast," says Dr. Giammanco.
Myth No. 4: Newer homes are automatically protected
As of 2019, some 60.3 million people lived in hurricane prone areas, up 16% (or an additional 8.3 million people) since 2000. With such population growth comes more homes, but even newer homes can have vulnerabilities. Inspect your property for:
- Loose or improperly installed roofing materials
- Unsealed windows and exterior doors
- Garage doors that aren't rated for high winds
- Areas where water can pool near the foundation
- Unsecured outdoor furniture and decorative features
- Trees or branches that could fall on the home
- Gaps around utility and HVAC penetrations
- Missing or damaged storm shutters and window protections
"What we know for sure is that once water gets into a home, damage starts multiplying quickly," says Dr. Giammanco. "Whether it's through a damaged roof, deteriorated flashing or an opening around a window, water intrusion can turn a relatively minor issue into a much larger and more expensive loss."
Myth No. 5: A small roof problem isn't urgent
Your roof can be a major weak spot in your home. Research from IBHS has shown that even minor roof issues can lead to substantial damage. "When the roof covering is lost and the roof deck is not sealed, significant amounts of water can enter a home very quickly," says Dr. Giammanco.
Before hurricane season is the best time to get your roof inspected, but late is better than never. Check your roof to expose:
- Roofing flashing vulnerabilities
- Missing, cracked or loose shingles
- Signs of leaks or water intrusion
- Soft spots, sagging or structural weakness
- Damaged roof vents and pipe boots
- Loose gutters and downspouts
- Clogged drainage areas that can cause water backup
- Tree limbs or debris that could damage the roof during high winds
- Worn sealants around chimneys, skylights and roof penetrations
- Areas that may be vulnerable to wind uplift during a hurricane
An inspection can ensure your entire roof is ready to withstand hurricane season, and save you hundreds if not thousands of dollars. "One loose piece of flashing can lead to thousands of dollars in water damage," says Dr. Giammanco.
Myth No. 6: Emergency prep can wait until a storm appears
You can never be too prepared for a hurricane. In fact, you should always be prepared for a major storm to appear, whether that prep is proactive home maintenance, reviewing evacuation plans and understanding your home's flood risk.
"Preparedness also needs to start well before a storm appears in the forecast," Dr. Giammanco says. "Knowing your flood and surge risk, understanding evacuation routes, and making home improvements ahead of hurricane season can make a significant difference when a storm approaches."
At the beginning of the season and prior to any mumbling of a storm, do the following:
- Build or restock your emergency supply kit
- Stock up on nonperishable food and bottled water
- Review and update your evacuation plan
- Gather important documents and store them in a waterproof container
- Test flashlights, lanterns and backup batteries
- Make sure generators are fueled and working properly
- Refill prescription medications and pet supplies
- Know your local evacuation routes and emergency shelters
Myth No. 7: Hurricane damage is unavoidable
If a devastating hurricane blows through, your home is likely to see some damage. But for category 1, 2 and 3 hurricanes, there are certainly some ways to stop preventable storm damage in its tracks, starting with tree trimming and roof flashing inspections.
"Both are relatively simple maintenance tasks that can go a long way toward reducing storm damage." says Dr. Giammanco. "Flashing helps keep water out at some of the roof's most vulnerable areas, and small issues can turn into costly leaks during a hurricane. Tree trimming is also important because overhanging branches can damage roofs, windows, and siding during high winds."
The hurricane checklist homeowners should complete this month
Before the next storm hits, complete these tasks so that your home is ready:
- Inspect roof flashing to protect against water damage.
- Trim tree limbs to prevent them from falling on your roof.
- Review evacuation plans so that you know exactly what to do if your area needs to evacuate.
- Know flood risk in your area.
- Review insurance coverage so you know what's covered.
- Secure outdoor items or move them indoors.
- Photograph valuables so that you have verifiable proof of damage.
Frequently asked questions
When is peak hurricane season?
Peak hurricane season is mid-August through the end of October.
Is wind or flooding more dangerous during a hurricane?
While both wind and flooding will damage your home, water-related hazards pose the greatest threat to human life (and your home). It's storm surges that are often the driver for evacuations.
Do inland homes need hurricane preparation?
Inland homes absolutely need hurricane preparation. Tropical storms can reach hundreds of miles inland, leading to flooding, high winds and power outages.
What is the most important home maintenance task before hurricane season?
Inspecting your roof is one of the most important home maintenance tasks to do before hurricane season. Even minor damage to your flashing can lead to major water damage if you are in the path of a hurricane or tropical storm.
Our editors independently choose our recommendations. Some content is produced with paid support from a third party, however our editorial decisions remain independent. If you buy through our links, the USA TODAY Network may earn a commission. Prices and availability may change.

title: When to expect king tides in Miami-Dade County, what to do if it floods
text:
When to expect king tides in Miami-Dade County, what to do if it floods
- South Florida's low-lying communities can fall victim to flooding for a number of reasons, including due to king tides.
- Over the next three days, king tides are expected in Miami-Dade, according to local authorities.
South Florida's low-lying communities can fall victim to flooding for a number of reasons, including due to king tides — which are "exceptionally high" tides, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Over the next three days, king tides are expected in Miami-Dade, say local authorities.
King tides usually last around 3 hours, according to the City of Miami Beach, and typically occur during September, October and November. King tides may prompt "sunny day flooding," which occurs when "streets, roads, and sidewalks" become temporarily flooded, "even when it is not raining."
"More severe flooding may result if king tides coincide with bad weather conditions such as heavy rains, strong winds or big waves," reads Miami-Dade County's website. "However, sea level rise is causing these tides to happen more frequently, to last longer and extend further inland than in the past."
When are king tides expected in Miami-Dade County?
The predicted dates in 2026 are based on NOAA's "Annual Prediction Tide Tables from the Virginia Key station," according to the city of Miami Beach, and are as follows:
- September 10-13
- September 26-30
- October 7-13* (Highest predicted tide: October 10)
- October 24-30* (Highest predicted tide: October 26 and 27)
- November 6-9
- November 23-26
The asterisks (*) denote the highest predicted tide.
What is a king tide?
A king tide is a "non-scientific term" often used to describe exceptionally high tides, according to NOAA.
Higher-than-normal tides usually occur during new or full moons, as well as when the moon is "at its perigee." Higher tides can also occur during specific seasons around the country.
Safety tips during king tide flooding
According to the City of Miami, the following safety precautions should be observed during king tide flooding:
- Do not drive through floodwater, as it can contain "unseen hazards," including trash and pollutants.
- If you do come in contact with flood water, clean your skin with soap and hot water.
- Do not park your vehicle in low-lying areas, and those that have "come into contact with floodwater should be checked and cleaned."
- Properties that are in low-lying areas should use "flood mitigation options," like sand bags.
Sarah Perkel is a South Florida Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network's Florida Connect team. You can get all of Florida’s best content directly in your inbox each weekday day by signing up for the free newsletter, Florida TODAY.

title: Sea level rise prompts plan to elevate thousands of Florida homes
text:
Sea level rise prompts plan to elevate thousands of Florida homes
- The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers recommends elevating 3,230 residential buildings in Miami-Dade County.
- Miami-Dade County is becoming "increasingly vulnerable" to flooding and storm damage, according to the Army Corps.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers plans to elevate more than 3,000 residential buildings in Miami-Dade County as the area becomes "increasingly vulnerable" to flood events due to the effects of climate change.
The Army Corps released a tentative plan to help flood-proof homes and critical infrastructure in "low-lying neighborhoods" throughout Miami-Dade County, as rising sea levels make them more vulnerable to flooding and storm damage. The proposal constitutes phase two of the larger "Back Bay" plan, which aims to protect the county's most vulnerable areas from storm damage.
Members of the public can submit their comments on the proposal until Sept. 18, according to the Army Corps.
How many Miami-Dade homes are in the elevation plan
The first phase of the plan consisted of a $2.7 billion project that would elevate 2,100 residential buildings and flood-proof 400 other structures, including hospitals and schools.
The second phase of the project recommends elevating up to 3,230 residential buildings, including "2,800 single-family homes and 430 smaller multifamily residential buildings," as well as floodproofing up to 175 nonresidential buildings and up to 100 "critical infrastructure facilities." About 1,500 of those residential buildings would be raised to around 11 feet above ground, with around 640 raised an estimated 12 feet above ground.
Phase two focuses on areas including Cutler Bay, El Portal, Florida City, Hialeah, Homestead, Miami, Miami Beach, Miami Shores, Miami Springs, and North Bay Village, as well as parts of unincorporated Miami-Dade County, according to the report.
According to the report, the total project cost is estimated at $6.65 billion, of which the federal government will bear 65%, or $4.32 billion. The non-federal share of costs is estimated at $2.33 billion.
The Army Corps hopes to receive congressional authorization in 2028, with the construction window estimated to begin in 2032.
Why Miami-Dade County is so flood-prone
Miami-Dade County is home to multiple low-lying areas that are at risk of flooding due to a number of reasons, including heavy rain, storm surge and king tides, according to the report, threats that "frequently disrupt lifeline services."
"The region’s extensive network of drainage canals provides direct pathways for tidal backflow and storm surge from Biscayne Bay to penetrate deep inland," reads the draft report on the project's second phase. "This risk is severely compounded by rising sea levels, which elevate the porous shallow groundwater table, reducing stormwater storage capacity and causing localized groundwater flooding."
Additionally, "recent regional tide gauge data from Virginia Key" confirms that local sea levels "are rising at an accelerated rate," which amplifies the "severity of future coastal storm risk."
Sarah Perkel is a South Florida Connect Reporter for the USA TODAY Network's Florida Connect team. You can get all of Florida’s best content directly in your inbox each weekday day by signing up for the free newsletter, Florida TODAY.

title: Hurricane Lowell wave topples meteorologist in Hawaii: Video
text:
Hurricane Lowell wave topples meteorologist in Hawaii: Video
Powerful ocean waves nearly toppled a meteorologist in Hawaii on Sept. 8 as Hurricane Lowell brought dangerous conditions to the islands.
Mike Seidel, a weather storm specialist for Fox Weather, was doing a live TV stand-up in Kauai, Hawaii, on Sept. 8 when a massive wave swept through the area.
In the clip, the camera operator points behind Seidel seconds before the wave hits.
The ocean's force makes both Seidel and the camera operator stumble and nearly fall. For several seconds, the camera angle jolts to a view of just gushing water.
But Seidel and the cameraperson both quickly recover. "We're okay," the meteorologist said before the camera operator flashed a thumbs-up.
Watch the moment in the video below.
Lowell latest: One dead in Hawaii, governor says
Lowell has been downgraded to a tropical storm as of Sept. 9. The National Hurricane Center said in a recent advisory that the storm will gradually weaken over the next few days.
Before being downgraded, Lowell, as a hurricane, passed close to the Hawaiian Islands, causing heavy winds, rainfall and widespread power outages.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green told CNN that one person, a homeless man on Oahu, died during the storm when a tree fell on him.
The storm's effects are expected to linger in the coming days. More than 32,000 are without power as of Sept. 9, according to USA TODAY's outage tracker.
The Hawaii Emergency Management Agency also warned residents about downed trees, utility poles and power lines.
"There’s a lot of damage on Kauaʻi and it’s going to take quite some time to get back to normal. The mayors are all working together and supporting one another and we’re going to continue doing everything we can to help people recover," Green said in a Sept. 8 news release.
Contributing: Gabe Hauari/ USA TODAY
Melina Khan is a national trending reporter for USA TODAY. Keep up with her on X @melinakh and Instagram @bymelinakhan.

title: Where is Tropical Storm Lowell headed? See latest path tracker
text:
Where is Tropical Storm Lowell headed? See latest path tracker
The worst of Lowell has passed for the Hawaiian Islands as the storm has been downgraded from a hurricane to a tropical storm, and the storm's path appears to be taking it away from the islands.
The storm brought damaging winds and heavy rainfall to the islands of Kauai and Oahu, with the Hawaii Emergency Management Agency reporting widespread power outages on both islands. According to a USA TODAY Power Outage Tracker, Kauai has over 32,000 reported outages, accounting for about 91% of total customers. The agency also said downed trees, utility poles and power lines have been reported across the island.
“People are really struggling. Keep them in your prayers, send resources and support them as you can,” said Hawaii Governor Josh Green in a Sept. 8 news release. “We’re getting people healthcare. We’re going to care for people the best way we can as we build our infrastructure back. There’s a lot of damage on Kauaʻi and it’s going to take quite some time to get back to normal. The mayors are all working together and supporting one another and we’re going to continue doing everything we can to help people recover.”
The National Hurricane Center said in its latest advisory that Lowell is weakening and moving away from the Hawaiian Islands. Forecasters said a slow turn toward the northwest then west is expected Wednesday into Thursday, Sept. 10.
Maximum sustained winds have decreased to around 65 mph with higher gusts, and gradual weakening is forecast during the next few days, according to the hurricane center. Swells from Lowell will continue to generate life-threatening surf and rip current conditions during the next day or so along exposed coasts of the Hawaiian Islands, forecasters said.
Tropical Storm Lowell path tracker
This forecast track shows the most likely path of the center of the storm. It does not illustrate the full width of the storm or its impacts, and the center of the storm is likely to travel outside the cone up to 33% of the time.
Tropical Storm Lowell spaghetti models
Illustrations include an array of forecast tools and models, and not all are created equal. The hurricane center uses only the top four or five highest-performing models to help make its forecasts.
Gabe Hauari is a national trending news reporter at USA TODAY. You can follow him on X @GabeHauari or email him at Gdhauari@usatoday.com.

title: See Hurricane Lowell path tracker, forecast, spaghetti models
text:
See Hurricane Lowell path tracker, forecast, spaghetti models
Hurricane Lowell is passing just west of Hawaii in the early morning hours of Sept. 8, according to the National Hurricane Center, bringing with it "damaging winds, heavy rainfall and powerful waves."
The latest advisory from the hurricane center said Lowell was passing just west of Niihau, the westernmost of the main Hawaiian Islands, with maximum sustained winds around 110 mph with higher gusts. After passing the Hawaiian Islands on Tuesday, Lowell is expected to turn toward the northwest and west and slow down on Wednesday, Sept. 9 and Thursday, Sept. 10, the NHC said.
A hurricane warning remains in effect for Kauai County, including the islands of Kauai and Niihau, where hurricane conditions began on the afternoon of Sept. 7. A tropical storm warning is also in effect for Oahu, according to the hurricane center.
Lowell is forecast to produce rainfall totals of 4 to 8 inches for Kauai, with maximum storm totals of 24 inches possible. For the Big Island, an additional 3 to 8 inches of rain is expected with isolated storm totals around 12 inches. Forecasters said Oahu and Maui could see an additional 2 to 5 inches of rain, with isolated storm totals around 10 inches.
The heavy rain could produce "significant flash flooding and mudslides, especially across Kauai and portions of the Big Island," hurricane center forecasters said.
Residents in flood-prone and coastal areas have been urged to move to safer locations or refuge areas if necessary, while emergency officials warned that power outages, road closures and disruptions to water service may occur as Lowell moves past the state.

title: Hurricane Lowell's twisted path takes another turn
text:
Hurricane Lowell's twisted path takes another turn
Powerful Hurricane Lowell passed close to the Hawaiian Islands overnight, but its rain, power outages and other dangers could linger into Sept. 9.
Lowell is rushing off to the north at 15 mph and forecast to take a twisting path out to sea. The storm completed a dramatic right turn in recent days and is now expected to be jostled onto a westward track.
Meanwhile, weather-related warnings remain in place in the islands, said Mike Brennan, the National Hurricane Center director.
Conditions on Kauai are "very dangerous" and there are "widespread power outages," Brennan said, making a plea for post-storm safety during a YouTube briefing update on Lowell. The hurricane and tropical storm warnings have been discontinued on Kauai and Oahu.
The islands continue to see some higher wind gusts — particularly at higher elevations, rain and dangerous surf that are expected to linger into the overnight hours on Sept. 8, Brennan said.
Rain of up to 5 inches on Kauai and 8 inches across the Big Island could "continue to produce some dangerous flash flooding and mudslides all the way through today and into Wednesday," Brennan warned.
Lowell passed to the west of the main Hawaiian Islands overnight and early Sept. 8.
What are the power outages like in Hawaii?
As Brennan noted, Lowell's strong winds wreaked havoc on power lines on Kauai. As of Tuesday morning, Sept. 8, utility providers on the island reported most of Kauai was without electricity. More than 33,268 customers were without electricity, roughly 93% of the total customers, according to USA TODAY's Outage Tracker.
About 7% of customers on Oahu were without electricity, about 7% of the island's total customers, according to the outage tracker.
How close did Hurricane Lowell get to Hawaii's main islands?
At its closest point overnight on Sept. 8, Lowell’s center passed just about 37 miles west of the western shore of Niihau and about 72 miles west of Waimea on Kauai’s southwest coast.
Hurricane Lowell path shows more twists, turns
As of 11 a.m. Hawaii time, or 5 p.m. ET on Sept. 8, Hurricane Lowell was centered about 230 miles north-northwest of Lihue, Hawaii, according to the National Hurricane Center. Its maximum sustained winds were 75 mph, just barely a hurricane.
Lowell is forecast to become a tropical storm later Sept. 8 as it rushes north. After that, the forecast is somewhat uncertain, Eric Blake, one of the center's hurricane specialists wrote in a forecast.
Lowell should gradually turn toward the west and slow down as its influenced by troughs and ridges in the atmosphere around it, then turn northward again, Blake wrote. It could take a turn similar to the one south of Hawaii that brought it into the island archipelago but not quite as much of a hard right.
Although slow weakening is forecast, some of the computer forecast models indicate Lowell could restrengthen over the weekend out in the open ocean.
Post storm safety tips from the hurricane center
"As dawn is breaking this morning, please be safe venturing outside," Brennan warned. "There are many hazards that remain. There are downed trees and power lines, debris, flood water, floodwaters that you want to be mindful of if you are going to be outside."
Here are other tips from Brennan and the weather service:
- If you evacuated, don't return until told it's safe to do so by local officials.
- Clean up safely, do not push yourself too hard and drink plenty of water
- Check on your neighbors
- Use generators outdoors and at least 20 feet away from your home to ensure proper ventilation
- Be careful near damaged buildings. Do not enter a damaged building until local authorities say it's safe.
- Leave your home if there's shifting or unusual noises.
- If you smell gas, get outdoors immediately and call 911.
- Stay far away from damaged power lines, whether they've fallen to the ground or are dangling overheard.
- Don't walk or drive through floodwaters.
Homes damaged, roads flooded amid Lowell
Several road closures were reported across the island chain thanks to the heavy rains and surging ocean, according to social media posts from state and local officials. The Hanalei Bridge on the north side of Kauai was closed on Labor Day morning because of flooding. Several waterways on the island shot up 6 to 8 feet during the heavy rain on Labor Day.
One person was injured in Kilauea on Kauai when a tree fell on a home, the weather service said. The following incidents also were reported by the weather service and other state and local officials:
- Dozens of homes were destroyed in Baby Beach in Poipu, on Kauai's south coast, the weather service said, including a home blown off its foundation and into a neighbor’s yard.
- The ocean surged into the pool of at least one resort in Poipu, encircled the building and covered the neighboring road in water, floating some cars away from their parking spots.
- In Kawaihau, emergency managers reported a roof was lifted off a home.
- On Oahu, the Honolulu Police Department closed a section of Farrington Highway after waves were reported crashing across all four lanes.
- On Maui, the Hawaii Department of Transportation closed the Honoapiilani Highway between Maalea and Olowalue after rocks and other debris covered the roadway.
Lowell prompts rare alert from the National Weather Service
When the National Weather Service in Honolulu issued a statewide tornado watch on Sept. 8, it was far from the first time that tornadoes have threatened Hawaii. However, it was the first time the office had issued a tornado watch, according to weather service meteorologist Maureen Ballard.
No reports were received of any tornadoes, and with the radar not working, there were no rotational signatures to investigate, the weather service told USA TODAY.
At least 40 tornadoes have been reported across the state since 1955, according to a USA TODAY analysis of NOAA’s historical tornado records. Only 13 of those were classified as a magnitude EF-1 or higher. Nine EF-1 tornadoes have been reported in the state and four EF-2s. All of those occurred between December and March.
The busiest month of the year for tornadoes is March, with 11 overall, according to the historical data.The Lowell-related tornado watch on Kauai expired on the morning of Sept. 8.
Heavy rain, flooding expected across parts of Hawaiian Islands
Forecasters warned that Lowell could continue to bring dangerous rainfall totals capable of producing significant flash flooding and landslides, especially on Kauai.
Additional rainfall of 4 to 8 inches is forecast for Kauai, with maximum storm totals of 24 inches, according to the National Hurricane Center. The Big Island could see 3 to 8 additional inches, with totals of 12 inches possible. Oahu and Maui County are expecting an additional 2 to 5 inches, with isolated storm totals of 10 inches possible.
Barking Sands on western Kauai clocked sustained winds of 51 mph, with a gust up to 84 mph, while Lihue Airport along the southeastern coast of Kauai saw sustained winds of 53 mph and a gust of 79 mph.
Emergency officials have repeatedly advised motorists not to drive through flooded roads.
Kauai County warns of utility disruptions
The county Department of Water issued a conservation notice, advising customers to limit water use to essential needs. Officials warned that power outages caused by the storm could affect pumps and wells, potentially reducing water pressure or causing service interruptions.
Residents were urged to store drinking water and fill containers for sanitation and other household needs before conditions worsen.
"Now is the time to shelter in place," Kawakami said Sept. 7. "Check in with your friends and neighbors, then hunker down until conditions let up on Tuesday."
Schools, parks and airport closed
As the storm closed in on the Hawaiian Islands, officials ordered a series of closures across Kauai. Public transit service on Kauai was suspended on Sept. 7, with buses instead supporting transportation to emergency refuge areas.
Lihue Airport closed on the afternoon of Sept. 7 ahead of the storm, according to Kauai County officials. All county and state offices on Kauai, along with Department of Education schools, are closed on Sept. 8.
County parks, campgrounds and the Wailua Golf Course have been closed until further notice, Kauai County officials said. State parks and forest reserves managed by the Department of Land and Natural Resources were also closed.
Ocean safety officials are urging residents and visitors to stay out of the water as large swells generated by Lowell create hazardous surf and rip current conditions around the islands.
"The public is reminded that refuge areas are evacuation options of last resort," Kauai County officials said. "In many cases, sheltering in place may be a good option, particularly if the home or structure is sound or hardened and located outside hazardous flood and storm-surge areas."
Hello, Norbert?
Unlike the sleepy Atlantic, there is no rest for the weary in the Pacific.
Far from Hawaii, Tropical Storm Marie is still spinning over the eastern Pacific Ocean far from land. Though well offshore and losing steam, swells from Marie are continuing to bring rough surf and dangerous rip currents to California beaches, the weather service said.
And looking ahead, storm activity in the Pacific Ocean will continue after Lowell zooms off into the sunset, hurricane center forecasters said on Sept. 8.
A developing system in the eastern Pacific could get the name Norbert if it becomes a named storm. The hurricane center is giving the system a 70% chance of development within the next seven days.
"Showers and thunderstorms associated with a broad area of low pressure located several hundred miles southwest of southwestern Mexico are showing signs of organization," the hurricane center said in a forecast released Sept. 8.
"Gradual development of this system is likely, and a tropical depression is expected to form later this week while the system moves generally west-northwestward at 10 to 15 mph."
While the Pacific basin remains active – due mainly to the hurricane-boosting effects of El Niño – the opposite is true in the Atlantic, which has only seen five tropical storms this year as we near the typical peak of the season. Looking ahead, the hurricane center said Sept. 8 that "tropical cyclone formation is not expected (in the Atlantic) during the next 7 days."
Contributing: Michael Loria and Yoonserk Pyun, USA TODAY

title: Hurricane Lowell approaches Hawaii as conditions worsen across islands
text:
Hurricane Lowell approaches Hawaii as conditions worsen across islands
The powerful storm is not expected to make a direct landfall but is still forecasted to bring serious weather to the islands.
Hurricane Lowell has put the western end of the Hawaiian Islands under a hurricane warning on Labor Day as it rapidly approaches with high winds, heavy rain, dangerous surf, and possible tornadoes.
"Flash flooding, damaging waves, and high winds are expected from Lowell," the National Hurricane Center warned in a late afternoon update on Sept. 7. The National Hurricane Center noted in its 8 p.m. ET advisory that conditions were deteriorating for the islands of Niihau, Kauai, and Oahu.
Lowell's center is not forecast to make a direct landfall on the main Hawaiian Islands as it passes on Sept. 7 and 8. Still, the threats have increased for the islands of Niihau and Kauai because the storm's forecast track has shifted steadily eastward, the National Hurricane Center said.
The hurricane warning – meaning hurricane conditions are expected within the watch area – is in effect for Kauai County, including the islands of Niihau and Kauai. A tropical storm warning – meaning tropical storm conditions are expected within the watch area – is in effect for Oahu, the most populated Hawaiian Island.
Forecasters expect Lowell to remain a hurricane as its center passes roughly 75 to 95 miles west of Niihau on Monday night and into Tuesday, Sept. 8, the National Weather Service in Honolulu said. Any additional eastward shifts in the track could bring even stronger winds and greater impacts to the islands.
In addition to the potential hurricane-force wind gusts, tornadoes are possible near the two islands, and heavy rains are expected throughout the main islands, the hurricane center's specialists warned. In Kauai County and the island of Hawaii, the rain could trigger flash floods and mudslides.
Tropical storm-force winds extend out up to 175 miles from the center of the storm. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 60 miles. A few tornadoes are also possible across the remainder of the Hawaiian Islands, forecasters said.
"Make sure everyone takes this seriously, especially on Kauai, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said in a Sept. 6 video posted to social media. Residents and visitors have been urged to closely monitor the weather and the watches or warnings as Lowell approaches the islands, the hurricane center said.
In a separate video, Kauai Mayor Derek Kawakami said: "We need the entire island to be vigilant."
"The ocean is going to be rough, so really, really be careful," Kawakami said, urging residents to remember that swells from the remnants of Hurricane Karina also will be arriving on northeast-facing shores.
Where is Hurricane Lowell?
At 8 p.m. ET, Hurricane Lowell was 230 miles southwest of Lihue on Kauai, and 275 miles west-southwest of Honolulu. Lowell weakened slightly with maximum sustained winds of 110 mph, making it a Category 2 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. The storm, moving to the north-northeast at 18 mph, is forecast to continue weakening.
Regardless of the category, Lowell is forecast to have sweeping impacts across the state as it passes to the west of Kauai and Niihau, officials and hurricane scientists warned. Hurricane conditions are expected in Kauai County beginning Monday afternoon, Sept. 7.
What's forecast for Hawaii?
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration offices, including the weather service and its hurricane center, expect the following impacts:
- Life-threatening winds across Niihau and Kauai, with possible extensive impacts, including damage to roofs and possible destruction of some mobile homes and large trees snapped or uprooted.
- Dangerous winds also could have limited to significant impacts across Oahu.
- Life-threatening surf and rip currents, as swells arrive from both Lowell and the remnants of Karina.
- Several tornadoes possible near Kauai and Niihau, and a few possible elsewhere.
- Storm surge of 1 to 3 feet on Kauai and up to 1 foot on Oahu, accompanied by large and destructive waves.
- Significant flash flooding and mudslides across Kauai County and portions of the Big Island (Hawaii County).
The following rainfall amounts are forecast:
- Kauai County: 6 to 10 inches, with isolated totals up to 14 inches
- Big Island: 4 to 8 inches of rain, with isolated totals up to 12 inches
- Maui: 4 to 8 inches of rain, with up to 10 inches possible
- Elsewhere in the islands: 2 to 4 inches
'Forbidden island' in Lowell's path
While the island of Kauai (population 73,000) is expected to feel Lowell's high winds, so could the tiny, lightly populated island of Niihau, about 17 miles southwest of Kauai.
Also known as the "forbidden island," the private island's population is very small, at roughly 70 people, as of the most recent census.
Niihau is the seventh-largest island in the Hawaiian Island chain, but the smallest populated island, according to the Niihau Cultural Heritage Foundation.
With no paved roads, no power grid, and limited contact with the outside world, Niihau "offers a glimpse of an older Hawaii," according to Hawaii.com. The Hawaiian language is still spoken daily, and subsistence living remains the way of life. Families on the island are known for making traditional shell leis.
The "forbidden" nickname dates back to the 19th century when outsiders were restricted from visiting to protect residents from disease and Western influence, Hawaii.com said. Even now, access is extremely limited. There are no hotels, restaurants, or shops anywhere on Niihau.
Contributing: Thao Nguyen and Karina Zaiets, USA TODAY

title: Lowell shifts east, prompting hurricane watch for Kauai and Niihau
text:
Lowell shifts east, prompting hurricane watch for Kauai and Niihau
Hawaii is expected to avoid a direct landfall from Hurricane Lowell, but the powerful storm is forecast to bring heavy rain, dangerous surf and possible tornadoes across the entire island chain as the center passes nearby on Labor Day and into Tuesday, Sept. 8.
As Lowell made its forecast turn to the north on Sunday, Sept. 6, the projected track kept shifting slightly east, prompting both a tropical storm warning and a hurricane watch for the islands of Kauai and Niihau, the National Hurricane Center said.
A warning means conditions are expected within 36 hours, and a watch means conditions are possible within the watch area. The eastward shift increased the chances of hurricane-force wind gusts on Niihau and possibly Kauai, especially at higher elevations, the hurricane center warned.
Several tornadoes are possible near Kauai and Niihau on Labor Day and overnight, and a few tornadoes are also possible across the remainder of the Hawaiian Islands, the hurricane center warned.
Forecasters expect Lowell to remain a hurricane as it nears the west end of the main Hawaiian Islands on Sept. 7. The latest forecast predicts the center will pass roughly 115 to 150 miles west of Kauai, close enough that any additional eastward shifts in the track could bring stronger winds and greater impacts, particularly to Kauai, the hurricane center said.
Tropical storm-force winds extend out up to 175 miles from the center of the storm. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 50 miles.
The entire island chain is forecast to receive heavy rain early in the week that could trigger flash flooding. Hawaii residents and visitors should continue monitoring forecasts and any watches or warnings that may be issued as Lowell approaches the islands, the hurricane center said.
Where is Hurricane Lowell?
At 5 p.m. HST on Sept. 6, Lowell made the northward turn and was accelerating, the hurricane center said in its latest advisory.
The storm was about 500 miles south-southwest of Lihue on Kauai, and about 525 miles southwest of Honolulu. Its maximum sustained winds had decreased to 120 mph, still a dangerous Category 3 hurricane.
Lowell is forecast to begin accelerating and move north to northeastward across portions of the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument before passing just west of the main Hawaiian Islands. Though gradual weakening is expected to begin by Sept. 7, Lowell is forecast to remain a hurricane as it nears the islands.
A hurricane warning is in effect for the marine monument between Niihoa and French Frigate Shoals.
Flood watch in place for portions of Hawaii
Moisture along the eastern flank of Hurricane Lowell is forecast to bring periods of heavy rain through Tuesday, Sept. 8, the National Weather Service said.
A flood watch is in effect through 6 p.m. HT on Sept. 8 for Maui, Lanai, Molokai, Oahu, The Big Island and Kahoolawe.
A flood watch means conditions are favorable for flash flooding but does not mean flooding will occur, said Oahu Emergency Management in a social media post.
Initially, the threat will be highest along windward and mountain areas, then spread everywhere by Sept. 7, the weather service said. Flood-prone roads and low-lying areas may be closed due to elevated runoff and overflowing streams, while urban areas may receive more significant flooding and property damage due to rapid runoff.
The Maui County Fire Department urged caution on beaches and shorelines as "larger-than-normal waves and stronger-than-usual currents may be present."
"This may not be the day for inexperienced ocean goers to enter the water," the fire department warned on Sept. 6.
What impacts could Hawaii see?
Heavy rain is expected across much of the state, with a 100% chance of rain on Labor Day.
For Kauai and the Big Island, 4 to 10 inches is forecast with isolated totals exceeding 14 inches. Maui could receive 2 to 4 inches, with locally higher amounts approaching 8 inches. Elsewhere, rainfall totals of 1 to 2 inches are expected.
The rain could trigger flash flooding and mudslides, particularly in mountainous areas.
Coastal impacts are also expected. Storm surge could raise water levels 1 to 3 feet above normally dry ground in Kauai County and up to 1 foot on Oahu if the highest water coincides with high tide. Large, destructive waves and life-threatening rip currents are forecast across many Hawaiian shorelines during the next several days.
How should residents prepare?
Emergency officials recommend using the weekend to finish hurricane preparations before conditions begin to deteriorate.
The National Hurricane Center and National Weather Service advise residents to know their evacuation zone, avoid driving through flooded roads, and monitor official forecasts for updates. NOAA also recommends having an emergency kit with food, water, medications, flashlights, batteries, and multiple ways to receive weather alerts in case power or cellular service is disrupted.
This story has been updated to add new information.
Reporter Anthony Thompson can be reached at ajthompson@usatodayco.com, or on X @athompsonUSAT

title: Hurricane Lowell forecast: Watches issued as storm nears Hawaii
text:
Hurricane Lowell forecast: Watches issued as storm nears Hawaii
Category 4 Hurricane Lowell is forecast to turn northward over the weekend and take a path uncomfortably close to Kauai on Labor Day.
Hurricane Lowell continued its trek near the Hawaiian Islands on Saturday, Sept. 5. The storm, a Category 4 with sustained 130 mph winds, is forecast to approach the islands Monday night, Labor Day. The center of the hurricane is expected to move just west of the main Hawaiian Islands.
The National Hurricane Center issued a tropical storm watch for Kauai County and a hurricane watch for portions of the Papahanaumokuakea Marine National Monument late Saturday.
The storm, now moving west-northwest at just 5 mph, is forecast to turn northward to north-northeastward with an increase in forward speed Sunday and Monday, the National Hurricane Center said in its latest update.
Lowell is expected to be "near major hurricane strength when it makes its closest approach to the Hawaiian Islands," the hurricane center said. A major hurricane has winds of at least 111 mph; Category 3, 4 and 5 storms are classified as major hurricanes.
"Any deviation eastward from its forecast track could bring more severe wind impacts, especially to Kauai County," the National Weather Service in Honolulu said.
Where is Hurricane Lowell now?
As of 5 p.m. Hawaii time on Sept. 5, the center of Lowell was about 630 miles south-southwest of Lihue on Kauai and 635 miles south-southwest of Honolulu. The storm had maximum sustained winds of 130 mph, making it a Category 4 storm.
The hurricane briefly restrengthened to a Category 5 storm on Friday, Sept. 4, with maximum sustained winds of 160 mph. Fluctuations in intensity are possible through the next day or so, followed by a gradual weakening trend Sunday and Monday.
Lowell's hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 60 miles from the center, and tropical storm-force winds extend outward up to 160 miles.
How close will Lowell get to Hawaii?
The models are coming into better focus on Lowell’s path near the islands, the hurricane center said at 11 a.m. ET on Sept. 5.
Most of the model guidance suggests the center will travel 100 to 200 nautical miles to the west of Kauai on Sept. 7. However, because two of the models that have performed well for Lowell are along the eastern side of the guidance, the hurricane center nudged the track forecast slightly east.
Hawaii rainfall forecast for Lowell
"Heavy rainfall is likely to impact most islands at some point during Lowell's passage," said the National Weather Service in Honolulu. Rain is forecast across the south slopes of Maui and the Big Island as early as the evening of Sept. 6, followed by the rest of Maui County and Oahu on the morning of Sept. 7, and Kauai that afternoon.
Lowell is expected to produce rainfall totals of 3 to 6 inches, with maximum totals exceeding 10 inches possible for Kauai and the Big Island, the hurricane center said. For Maui, 2 to 4 inches of rain is expected, with isolated maximum totals of 8 inches possible.
Across the remaining islands, rainfall of 1 to 2 inches with maximum amounts of 4 inches is possible.
This rainfall may produce flash flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain. The weather service said the locally higher rain amounts are expected on south and southeast slopes.
Storm surge also expected
The combination of storm surge and tides could cause normally dry coastal areas to flood. The National Hurricane Center said water could reach 1 to 3 feet above ground in Kauai County and up to a foot in Oahu, if peak surge occurs at the time of high tide.
The deepest water is expected along the immediate coast near and to the right of the center, where the surge could be accompanied by large and destructive waves.
Rough surf also expected
Swells from two storms are expected to affect the Hawaiian Islands over Sept. 5 and Sept. 6, and early in the week.
Swells from Lowell are expected to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions in portions of the Islands during the next several days. High surf advisories are in place for all south- and east-facing shores in Hawaii, as well as the west shore of the Big Island, under the influence of Lowell and Hurricane Karina.
Southerly swells from Lowell are forecast to bring high surf advisories to the islands through Saturday, Sept. 5, while Karina is producing high surf on east-facing shores.
The weather service said confidence is beginning to increase for the potential for extra-large surf along south and western exposures early next week. Coinciding with monthly high tides, the surf will create the potential for impacts to harbor entrances and channels, as well as coastal properties and roads.
As Karina disintegrates, an easterly swell from the gale from the remnants of former Hurricane Karina is expected through Sept. 6, with higher seas, winds and chances of rain on the night of Sept. 7 and on Sept. 8 as that gale moves through the area, the weather service said.
Track Lowell
Beware the right-front quadrant
The current projected path of Lowell shows it zooming to the north, likely impacting Kauai on Sept. 7. This will bring the storm's right front quadrant toward Kauai.
Why is this important? "The winds, storm surge and even tornadic activity tend to be more extreme or prevalent in the right-front quadrant," said University of Georgia meteorologist Marshall Shepherd recently in Forbes magazine.
This is because the storm's forward motion adds to its rotating winds, producing the highest wind speeds and often the worst surge and tornado threat, according to Weather.com meteorologist Chris Dolce.
What are the wind chances in the Hawaiian Islands?
The hurricane center's current forecast indicates the following probabilities for tropical storm-force winds on Sept. 7 to Sept. 8. The wind chances increased with an eastward shift in the forecast Sept. 5.
- 86% – Nihoa (150 miles northwest of Kauai)
- 38% – Niihau
- 30% – Barking Sands (west side of Kauai)
- 17% – Lihue, Kauai
- 2% – Honolulu
The island of Nihoa also has up to a 76% chance of 58-mph winds on Tuesday, Sept. 8, and a 51% chance of hurricane-force winds, while the chances for those higher winds on the outlying islands of Necker and Niihau are in the single digits, the hurricane center said. Barking Sands, a beach on the western shore of Kauai, has a 1% chance of hurricane force winds.
Hurricane safety tips
This weekend would be a good time for Hawaii residents to review hurricane safety plans.
The weather service notes that storm surge and inland flooding remain the deadliest hurricane hazards and urged people to know their evacuation zone, follow evacuation orders and never drive on flooded roads. Several storm-related fatalities in 2026 have been linked to motorists attempting to cross flooded roadways.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration also recommends assembling an emergency kit that includes at least three days of water (1 gallon per person per day), nonperishable food, medications, flashlights, batteries, cash and a battery-powered or hand-cranked weather radio.
NOAA further advises having multiple ways to receive emergency warnings rather than relying solely on a cellphone. Options include weather radios, emergency alert systems, television and radio broadcasts, and trusted weather apps.

title: South Florida likely to see rainy Labor Day weekend. Here's when
text:
South Florida likely to see rainy Labor Day weekend. Here's when
- South Florida is likely to see rainy weather over the course of this upcoming Labor Day weekend, according to the National Weather Service Forecast Office Miami-South Florida.
- Chances of precipitation are 80% on Labor Day in Miami and Fort Lauderdale, and 60% in West Palm Beach.
South Florida is likely to see rainy weather over the course of this upcoming Labor Day weekend, according to the National Weather Service Forecast Office Miami-South Florida.
On Saturday, Miami will see a 50% chance of showers and thunderstorms, an 80% chance of precipitation on Sunday, as well as an 80% chance of precipitation on Labor Day, with showers and thunderstorms expected after 2 p.m.
Fort Lauderdale will see a 50% chance of showers and thunderstorms, especially after 1 p.m. on Saturday, with a slight chance of showers and thunderstorms on Sunday, as well as an overall chance of precipitation of 80%. On Labor Day itself, the city is likely to see showers and thunderstorms, mainly after 2 p.m., with an 80% chance of precipitation.
In West Palm Beach, Saturday has a 60% chance of precipitation, with showers and thunderstorms likely between 3 p.m. and 5 p.m. Sunday will likely see showers and thunderstorms, especially after 2 p.m., with a 70% chance of precipitation. On Labor Day, there's a chance of showers and thunderstorms in the area, with an 80% chance of precipitation.
